metadata.title: Expanding Brackets and Factorising Linear Expressions
metadata.vcaa_description: Create, expand, factorise, rearrange and simplify linear expressions, applying the associative, commutative, identity, distributive and inverse properties.
metadata.target_mastery: Apply the distributive law to expand single and multiple bracketed terms (including negative multipliers) and factorise algebraic expressions by extracting the Highest Common Factor (HCF).
prerequisites: Collecting like terms and multiplying algebraic terms (Section 5A)

key_vocabulary.definition: Multiplying a sum or difference inside brackets by an outside factor multiplies every term inside the brackets by that factor: $a(b + c) = ab + ac$.
Rewriting a bracketed algebraic expression as a sum or difference of terms without brackets.
The inverse of expanding: rewriting a sum of terms as a product by extracting the Highest Common Factor (HCF) outside brackets.

theory.title: The Distributive Law and Expanding Brackets
theory.explanation: Geometrically, a rectangle of height $a$ and split width $(b + c)$ has total area $a(b + c)$, which equals the sum of the two smaller rectangular areas $ab + ac$. When the term outside the brackets is negative, multiplying each inside term by that negative factor reverses the sign of every term inside the brackets.
theory.formula_latex: a(b + c) = ab + ac, \quad -a(b - c) = -ab + ac
theory.callout_title: Negative Outside Flips Every Sign Inside
theory.callout_rule: When expanding $-3(2x - 5)$, multiply $-3$ by BOTH $+2x$ and $-5$: $-3(2x) + (-3)(-5) = -6x + 15$. A standalone minus sign in front of brackets means $-1$: $-(x - 4) = -x + 4$.

theory.title: Expanding and Collecting Like Terms
theory.explanation: When an expression contains two or more bracketed groups, expand each bracket separately (keeping careful track of the sign attached to each outside multiplier) and then simplify by collecting like terms.
theory.callout_title: Treat the Sign in Front of the Multiplier as Part of It
theory.callout_rule: In $4(2x - 1) - 3(x - 5)$, the second multiplier is $(-3)$, not $+3$.

theory.title: Factorising Linear and Quadratic-Term Expressions Using the HCF
theory.explanation: Factorising is the reverse process of expanding. First find the Highest Common Factor (HCF) of both the numerical coefficients and the pronumeral parts across all terms. Place the HCF in front of a pair of brackets, and divide each original term by the HCF to obtain the terms inside the brackets. If the leading term is negative, factor out a negative HCF.
theory.callout_title: Expand Mentally to Check Every Factorisation
theory.callout_rule: You can always verify a factorisation immediately by expanding your brackets mentally to check that it reproduces the original expression!

worked_examples.title: Expanding Brackets with Positive and Negative Multipliers

steps.thinking: In part (a), multiply both $3x$ and $-4$ inside the brackets by $5$.
In part (b), multiply both $2a$ and $-7$ by $-4a$. Note that $(-4a) \times (-7) = +28a$.
Expand the first bracket by multiplying by $+3$, and the second bracket by multiplying by $-2$ (note that $-2 \times (-6) = +12$).
Collect the like terms in $x$ ($12x - 10x$) and the constant terms ($-9 + 12$).

worked_examples.title: Factorising by Extracting Positive and Negative HCFs

steps.thinking: In part (a), $\text{HCF}(18, 24) = 6$ and the common pronumeral factor is $m$, so the algebraic HCF is $6m$. Divide each term by $6m$.
In part (b), both terms are negative, so extract the negative HCF $-5$. Dividing $-25$ by $-5$ gives $+5$ inside the brackets.

common_misconceptions.title: Forgetting to Multiply the Second Term Inside the Brackets
common_misconceptions.misconception: Expanding $4(x + 5)$ as $4x + 5$, multiplying only the first term by $4$.
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: The outside factor $4$ multiplies the ENTIRE bracketed sum $(x + 5)$, so both $x$ and $5$ must be multiplied by $4$: $4(x + 5) = 4x + 20$.

common_misconceptions.title: Failing to Flip the Second Sign When Expanding a Negative Multiplier
common_misconceptions.correct_concept: A negative multiplier changes the sign of every term inside the brackets: $-3(x - 4) = -3x + 12$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Expand $7(2x - 5)$.
step_by_step_solution: Multiply each term inside the brackets by $7$.

fluency_and_understanding.question: Factorise completely $-18p^2 - 27pq$.
step_by_step_solution: Both terms are negative with $\text{HCF}(18, 27) = 9$ and shared pronumeral $p$, so extract $-9p$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A rectangular swimming pool in Mildura has width $4\text{ m}$ and length $(2x + 3)\text{ m}$. A paved deck along the side has width $3\text{ m}$ and length $(x + 5)\text{ m}$. Write an expanded and simplified algebraic expression for the combined area of the pool and deck, and evaluate it when $x = 5\text{ m}$.
step_by_step_solution: Write the sum of the two rectangular areas: $A = 4(2x + 3) + 3(x + 5)$.
Expand and collect like terms: $A = 8x + 12 + 3x + 15 = 11x + 27\text{ m}^2$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A Melbourne school hires $4$ buses for a Year 8 camp. Each bus carries $(3n - 2)$ students and $3$ teachers. Write an expanded expression for the total number of people on the $4$ buses.
step_by_step_solution: The number of people on each bus is $(3n - 2) + 3 = 3n + 1$.

problem_solving_and_modelling.question: A large rectangle of width $5x$ and length $(3x + 4)$ has a smaller rectangular cutout of width $2x$ and length $(x - 3)$ removed from its interior. Find an expanded and simplified expression for the remaining shaded area.
step_by_step_solution: Write the difference of the two areas: $A = 5x(3x + 4) - 2x(x - 3)$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: A student factorised $12x - 18$ as $3(4x - 6)$. Explain why this factorisation is incomplete and state the fully factorised form.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: $4x$ and $6$ still share a factor of $2$; complete factorisation is $6(2x - 3)$
step_by_step_solution: In $3(4x - 6)$, the terms inside the brackets ($4x$ and $-6$) still share a common factor of $2$, because $3$ is not the Highest Common Factor of $12$ and $18$.

reasoning_and_communication.question: Use the distributive law to explain how you can mentally calculate $7 \times 98$ by writing $98 = 100 - 2$.
Prove that for any integer $n$, the expression $5(2n + 3) - 2(n - 1) - 1$ is always a multiple of $8$.
reasoning_and_communication.final_answer: Simplifies to $8n + 16 = 8(n + 2)$, which is a multiple of $8$
step_by_step_solution: Factor out the HCF of $8$: $8(n + 2)$. Since $n + 2$ is an integer, $8(n + 2)$ is always a multiple of $8$.
